doc.title: Konitz Lee — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Whether the Tristano music was ever a working band
summary: They return to Gioia and Tristano's influence on musicians rather than public, and whether Lennie wanted a band.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: [Kirchner passes the photo album to Ken Kimery]
Let me address what you talked about last night, the Ted Gioia thing. He came to a conclusion that I don’t agree with that the Tristano-style music was “frigid” or something.
However he also uses terms such as “extraordinary body of work” and “visionary artists.” That ain’t bad. I understand what you’re saying . . .
He’s just saying that all of that might be true but “I don’t dig it.” That’s what it sounds like to me.

Maybe. I don’t want to pretend to read Ted’s mind and I don’t agree that music is “frigid” but I think he does respect the value of it. I think what he’s saying in large part is that the biggest influence was on other musicians rather than on the listening public. Do you agree with that or disagree with it?
As far as being more of an influence on musicians?
At some point, I think when we had the professional picture made in uniforms, there was a thought that this might be a working band. So that’s obviously a truth. It wasn’t a working band.
I never got the impression that Lennie really wanted to have a working band. Is that a fair statement?
